newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's new government polishes budget plans.
newsitem.headline: France's new government polishes budget plans.

text.p: Barely a month and a half after taking office, France's Socialist-led government is putting the final touches to 1997 budget plans which could set the tone for national budgets across Europe ahead of monetary union.

Government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann said on Wednesday Prime Minister Lionel Jospin would meet his ministers on Thursday to review measures designed to curb the budget deficit ahead of the release on Monday of an audit of public finances.

The measures, and results of the audit, are being watched closely to see how far the government, which condemned austerity in its election campaign, is prepared to go to bring the deficit towards three percent of gross domestic product to qualify for a single European currency.

Many expect it to target a deficit level of around 3.3 percent of GDP, above the 3.0 percent forecast by the previous centre-right government, but below the 3.5 percent or so expected to be estimated by the audit.

The government may also announce on Monday after the release of the audit that it plans to curb the deficit further next year to three percent of GDP in order to allay fears among its European partners about the overshoot this year.

"We must send a signal to our European partners to show willingnesss to respect Maastricht criteria, but according to our own interpretation," Didier Migaud, secretary to the parliament's influential finance committee, told reporters.
"I think the government will continue to post a target of three percent, though this would be more as regards the 1998 budget than that of 1997," he added.
Trautmann declined to give a figure for the likely size of the budget deficit to be forecast in the audit, being carried out by two members of the independent Court of Auditors.
And government ministers have refused to give details of any measures planned to curb the deficit.
"We have a working meeting tomorrow which will examine the measures which could accompany the estimates (in the audit)," Trautmann told a news conference after a cabinet meeting.
"The prime minister will then, make a decision on the different measures he wants to take," she said.
Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn has said any measures implemented could affect companies and well-off households, and involve budget savings.
But any measures affecting companies would be set up in such a way as not to hinder business investment, badly needed to revive economic growth.
He told reporters on Wednesday he had asked ministers to look for savings in all their budgets and said no areas of spending would be regarded as taboo.

The budgetary plans of the French government, brought to power in a surprise parliamentary election victory on June 1, will set the tone for a decision due in April/May next year on which countries can join a single currency.

The belief that France would be allowed to join with a deficit of some 3.3 percent of GDP has fuelled widespread expectations that the April/May decision will be based on a flexible reading of the Maastricht treaty.
That would allow other countries like Italy, which may also fall short of a strict reading of Maastricht treaty criteria, to argue their way in to a single currency from the start.

Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, in a radio interview earlier on Wednesday, said however countries should try to get as close to three percent as possible to reduce potential conflict over monetary union membership.

"Even if the Maastricht treaty leaves some room, the nearer we are to three percent, the less discussion there will be, and therefore I think everybody has an interest in working towards that," he told French radio.
